newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl urges calm in squabbling German coalition.
newsitem.headline: Kohl urges calm in squabbling German coalition.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl urged his shaken 14-year coalition to calm down on Monday as his liberal Free Democratic partners hammered away at Finance Minister Theo Waigel over a tax feud splitting the government.
Without mentioning the embarrassing feud, Kohl told his Christian Democrats (CDU) he firmly backed Waigel's efforts to cut state spending to qualify for Europe's single currency.

But while he also called for cooperation with the FDP, the pro-business party bitterly attacked Waigel for forcing it last week to give up a promised tax cut that it considered one of its major achievements in recent years.
The sudden storm in his centre-right coalition overshadowed the CDU annual congress only 10 days before Kohl sets a new record as postwar Germany's longest-serving chancellor.

"Of course, this or that could be improved in our coalition, despite all its successes," Kohl reassured the 1,000 delegates in Hanover, many of whom privately expressed concern about the damage the tax feud did to the government's image.

But, looking forward to the next election, he argued that the FDP had to have some victories to satisfy its voters too. He added: "Our goal is clear -- we want to continue this coalition of the centre beyond 1998."

FDP economics spokesman Otto Lambsdorff accused Waigel of ignoring his warnings that the 1997 budget was shaky and then reacting in panic when the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) refused to let him put off a promised rise in child benefits.
"Now he has to rush around and find funds to fill that hole," Lambsdorff told the Berliner Zeitung. "We feel we were pushed into a corner by this poor preparation for the budget."
FDP general-secretary Guido Westerwelle charged Waigel "disturbed the peace more and more" in the coalition because of power struggles within his Christian Social Union (CSU) party.

Kohl's coalition flirted with collapse last week when Waigel and the FDP battled over a possible petrol tax increase to fill gaps in the 1997 budget. As Germany's self-styled tax-cutting party, the FDP was firmly against it.
They finally agreed to delay a planned cut in the hated solidarity tax to help rebuild the ex-communist east.

Lambsdorff said the FDP would have left the government if Waigel had insisted on raising the petrol tax but added: "We don't want to dissolve the coalition today because we don't see any other partner we could work better with."
Kohl said his government's planned tax reform, which was due to be discussed at the congress on Tuesday, would not be introduced until 1999. The FDP and SPD want it in 1998.

The chancellor, 66, also called for a consensus between employers and unions over another controversial part of his austerity drive. Workers staged wildcat strikes last month when companies tried to impose a cut in sick pay benefits.
In a very short section on foreign affairs, Kohl reiterated his support for Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU) and said the EU had to expand eastwards.
Kohl, who has been CDU chairman for the past 23 years, was easily reelected as party leader for another two years with 95.5 percent support in a vote with no challenger.

The two-day congress also voted to introduce a women's quota, a key reform Kohl has championed to attract more women to a party whose membership is three-quarters male. The quota calls for one-third of the candidates for any party post to be women.
